name: St. Stephen's Day
description: The first Christian martyr is stoned for his faith.
biblicalBasis: Stephen, full of grace and power, performs signs and wonders (Acts 6:8-15). He delivers a defense speech in which he recounts Israel's salvation history and accuses the people of betraying and killing the Righteous One (Acts 7:1-53). He sees heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. While being stoned, he prays: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" and "Lord, do not hold this sin against them" (Acts 7:54-60).
significance: The placement on the day after Christmas is deliberate—it reveals the cost of faith. The joy of God's coming into the world is immediately confronted by the world's rejection. Stephen's prayer for his enemies mirrors Jesus' words from the cross and demonstrates the witness of martyrdom: faith stands firm even in the face of death.
liturgicalContext: Red liturgical color (martyr day). One of the oldest saint days in the church. In Scandinavian tradition also called "Second Day of Christmas". The contrast between the joy of Christmas and the solemnity of martyrdom is intentional in the liturgical calendar.
history: St. Stephen's Day has been celebrated on December 26 since the 400s. Stephen is regarded as the first martyr (protomartyr). The placement right after Christmas underscores the early church's awareness that the incarnation leads to the cross. Saulus (Paul) was present at the stoning—a detail that links martyrdom with mission.
otConnections: Stephen's speech reviews the entire Old Testament salvation history from Abraham to Solomon. He draws lines from Moses, who was rejected by his people, to Jesus, who was also rejected. The theme of opposition: as the fathers persecuted the prophets, so now the people persecute the Messiah and his witnesses.
